snail.e: From Middle English snayl, snail, from the Old English sneġel, from Proto-Germanic *snagilaz.
snail.g: Any of very many animals (either hermaphroditic or nonhermaphroditic), of the class Gastropoda, having a coiled shell.

snake.e: From Middle English snake, from Old English snaca (“snake, serpent, reptile”), from Proto-West Germanic *snakō (“slider, snake”), from *snakan (“to creep, slide”), related to Old High German snahhan (“to sneak, slide”).
snake.g: Any of the suborder Serpentes of legless reptiles with long, thin bodies and fork-shaped tongues.

snap.e: From Dutch snappen (“to bite; seize”) or Low German snappen (“to bite; seize”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *snappōn, from Proto-Germanic *snappōną (“to snap; snatch; chatter”), intensive form of *snapāną (”to snap; grab”, whence Old Norse snapa (“to get; scrounge”)), from Proto-Indo-European *snop-; compare Lithuanian snãpas (“beak, bill”).
snap.g: A quick breaking or cracking sound or the action of producing such a sound.

snare.e: From Middle English snare, from Old English sneare (“snare, noose”), from Proto-West Germanic *snarhā, from Proto-Germanic *snarhǭ (“a sling; loop; noose”).
snare.g: A trap (especially one made from a loop of wire, string, or leather).

snarl.e: From Middle English snarlen, frequentative of snaren (“to trap, tangle”). Equivalent to snare + -le.
snarl.g: To entangle; to complicate; to involve in knots.

snarl.e: Frequentative of earlier snar (“to growl”), perhaps from Middle Low German snorren (“to drone”), of probably imitative origin. Equivalent to snar + -le.
snarl.g: To growl angrily by gnashing or baring the teeth; to gnarl; to utter grumbling sounds.

snatch.e: From Middle English snacchen, snecchen (“to snap; seize”), from Old English *snæċċan, *sneċċan, from Proto-West Germanic *snakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *snakjaną (“to whiff, sniff, catch wind of; to taste-test, nibble”), related to Proto-Germanic *snakōną (“to breathe, blow, sigh”) and *snakkōną (“to blather, jabber, chatter”).

sneer.e: From Middle English sneren (“to mock, scoff at”), from Old English fnǣran (“to snort”), from Proto-West Germanic *fnāʀijan, from Proto-Germanic *fnesaną (“to pant, gasp”).
sneer.g: To raise a corner of the upper lip slightly, especially in scorn.

sneeze.e: From Middle English snesen (“to sneeze”), alteration of earlier fnesen (“to sneeze”), from Old English fnēosan (“to sneeze, snort”), from Proto-West Germanic *fneusan, from Proto-Germanic *fneusaną, from Proto-Indo-European *pnew- (“to breathe, pant, snort, sneeze”).
sneeze.g: To expel air as a reflex induced by an irritation in the nose.

sniff.e: From Middle English sniffen, of imitative origin.
sniff.g: To make a short, audible inhalation, through the nose, as when smelling something; to smell (something).

snort.e: From Middle English snorten, from earlier fnorten, from Old English *fnorettan, related to Middle English snoren, fnoren, from Old English fnora.
snort.g: The sound made by exhaling or inhaling roughly through the nose.

snout.e: From Middle English snowte, snout, snute, from Old English *snūt, *snūte or Middle Low German snûte, from Proto-West Germanic *snūt, from Proto-Germanic *snūtaz.
snout.g: The long, projecting nose, mouth, and jaw of a beast, as of pigs.

snow.e: Verb etymology 1, verb sense 2.3.2 (“to convince or hoodwink (someone)”) probably refers to a person being blinded or confused by a snowstorm. The adjective comes from the phrase a snowball's chance in hell, also see snowball clause at Wikipedia.
snow.g: The partly frozen, crystalline state of water that falls from the atmosphere as precipitation in flakes; also, the falling of such flakes; a

snow.e: Borrowed from Dutch snauw, snaauw, or Low German snau; further etymology uncertain, possibly from Low German snau (“beak”), related to Middle Low German snute (“snout”) (whence English snout), from Proto-West Germanic *snūt (“snout”), from Proto-Germanic *snūtaz (“snout”), possibly imitative.
snow.g: A square-rigged sailing vessel similar to a brig formerly used as a warship, with a foremast, a mainmast, and a trysail mast immediately aba

snows.e: From snow + -s (suffix forming pluralia tantum and regular plurals of nouns; and the third-person singular indicative present tense of verbs).
snows.g: One or both regions of the Earth where it snows the year round; the Arctic and/or Antarctic.

snowy.e: From Middle English snowy, snawy; from Old English snāwiġ. By surface analysis, snow + -y.
snowy.g: Marked by snow; characterized by snow.

snuff.e: Late Middle English, from Middle Dutch snuffen (“to snuff, sniff, snuffle”).
snuff.g: Finely ground or pulverized tobacco (or other plant derivative) intended for use by being sniffed or snorted into the nose.

snuff.e: From Middle English snoffe, snuffe, of uncertain origin.
snuff.g: The burning part of a candle wick, or the black, burnt remains of a wick (which must be periodically removed).

snuffer.g: A device made to extinguish (snuff out) a candle.
